lead: The ideal gas law pv = RT is the simplest equation of state: it links pressure, molar volume and temperature through one constant. It is accurate for air, nitrogen and carbon dioxide at room temperature and near-atmospheric pressure, and it underlies every cycle calculation in Unit 6. It fails near saturation and at high pressure, where molecules crowd together and pull on each other. Real-gas equations of state repair that by adding two corrections: a molecular volume and an attraction term. Compressor design, gas pipelines and cylinder filling all need the corrected form.
prereq: You need: state, property and equilibrium (Unit 1); pv = RT and specific heats (Unit 2); and the phase-change picture in 5.1.

blocks.text: An equation of state is any relation among pressure, volume and temperature for a fixed mass. The ideal gas is the simplest such model. Its molecules are treated as point masses: they occupy no volume of their own, they exert no force on one another except at the instant of a collision, and every collision is perfectly elastic. A gas behaves this way because at ordinary pressure it is mostly empty space.

blocks.where: p is absolute pressure in Pa; v is molar volume V/n in m³/mol; R_u is the universal gas constant, 8.314 J/(mol·K); T is absolute temperature in K, never °C.

blocks.text: Engineers usually work per kilogram, not per mole. Dividing R_u by molar mass M gives the specific gas constant R, and the law becomes pV = mRT. For air M = 0.02897 kg/mol, so R = 8.314/0.02897 = 287 J/(kg·K) = 0.287 kJ/(kg·K). For carbon dioxide M = 0.044 kg/mol, so R = 8.314/0.044 = 188.9 J/(kg·K).

blocks.where: V is total volume in m³; m is mass in kg; R is the specific gas constant in J/(kg·K); R_u = 8.314 J/(mol·K) is the universal gas constant; M is molar mass in kg/mol.

blocks.text: The same law defines a temperature scale. In a constant-volume gas thermometer, p at fixed v rises in proportion to T. Measuring p at the triple point of water (273.16 K, see 5.2) and then at the unknown state gives T = 273.16 × (p/p_tr). This is the ideal gas temperature scale; it agrees with the thermodynamic scale of Unit 3 for a gas at low pressure.

Two facts spoil the model. First, a molecule has a finite size, so the space available to it is less than the container volume. Second, molecules attract each other at short range, so a molecule about to strike the wall is pulled back and hits with less force. The first effect raises pressure; the second lowers it.

Deviations grow as the gas is compressed towards saturation, or pushed to high pressure at a temperature well above the critical temperature. At 1 atm and 300 K, carbon dioxide is within a fraction of a percent of ideal; at 5 MPa it is off by about 30 percent (Z ≈ 0.7). Near the saturated vapour line the ideal law can be wrong by tens of percent, because molecules are close to condensing.

A real gas, also called a non-ideal gas in some syllabi, therefore needs a better equation of state. The measure of the error is the compressibility factor Z = pv/(R_u T), covered in 5.7. For an ideal gas Z = 1 at every state.

Van der Waals repaired the ideal law with two constants. The constant b subtracts the volume the molecules themselves occupy, so the free volume becomes (v − b). The term a/v² restores the pressure lost because attraction pulls the molecules inward, away from the wall. Adding a/v² to the measured p gives the pressure the gas would exert if attraction were absent.

blocks.where: p is pressure in Pa; v is molar volume in m³/mol; T is in K; R_u = 8.314 J/(mol·K); a is the attraction constant in Pa·m⁶/mol²; b is the excluded volume in m³/mol, roughly four times the molecular volume.

blocks.text: Rearranged for pressure it is easier to use: p = R_u T/(v − b) − a/v². Both constants are found by fitting measured data, usually from the critical point.

items: Convert the given mass or moles to molar volume: v = V/n.
Subtract b from v to get the free volume, then compute R_u T/(v − b).
Subtract a/v² from that result to get p. Do the arithmetic in SI units, then convert to kPa or bar.

blocks.text: Van der Waals is the simplest real-gas equation, not the most accurate. Redlich–Kwong and Beattie–Bridgeman are better; they carry more constants and are fitted over wider ranges. Only a few universities teach them in detail, and most examinations ask for van der Waals with its constants supplied.

figure.caption: For one mole of carbon dioxide at 300 K the two curves almost overlap; at v = 0.024 m³/mol the ideal law gives 103.93 kPa and the van der Waals equation gives 103.48 kPa.

spec.aria: Two pressure-volume curves for one mole of carbon dioxide at 300 kelvin almost overlap: the ideal curve and the van der Waals curve differ slightly near 0.024 cubic metres per mole.

examples.question: One mole of carbon dioxide is held at 300 K in a tank of volume 0.024 m³. Take R_u = 8.314 J/(mol·K), a = 0.3640 Pa·m⁶/mol² and b = 4.267 × 10⁻⁵ m³/mol. Find the pressure from the ideal gas law and from the van der Waals equation, in kPa.
steps: Van der Waals form for pressure: p = R_u T/(v − b) − a/v².
Van der Waals pressure: p = 104 110.1 − 631.9 = 103 478.2 Pa.
examples.answer: Ideal p = 103.93 kPa and van der Waals p = 103.48 kPa; attraction lowers the pressure by about 0.45 kPa.
examples.check:
R_u = 8.314
T = 300.0
v = 0.024
a = 0.3640
b = 4.267e-5
p_ideal = R_u*T/v
p_vdw = R_u*T/(v - b) - a/v**2
print(round(p_ideal/1000, 2))
print(round(p_vdw/1000, 2))

traps: Using the total volume V in place of v in the van der Waals equation. There v is molar volume V/n, so for 4 mol in 0.024 m³ you must put v = 0.006 m³/mol.
Mixing units of a, b and R. If a is in Pa·m⁶/mol² and b in m³/mol, R must be 8.314 J/(mol·K) and p comes out in Pa, not kPa.
Putting T in °C. Both ideal and van der Waals equations need absolute temperature, so add 273.15 before substituting.
Using R_u where R is wanted. Divide by molar mass for per-kilogram work; 8.314 in pV = mRT with m in kg gives wrong numbers.
Claiming the van der Waals equation is exact near the critical point. It is a two-constant model, good for trends, and the compressibility chart of 5.7 is preferred for accurate work.

quiz.q: State the three assumptions of the ideal gas model.
quiz.a: Molecules have negligible volume; they exert no forces on each other except during collisions; collisions are perfectly elastic.

quiz.q: Write the relation between the universal and specific gas constants, and find R for carbon dioxide (M = 44 kg/kmol).
quiz.a: R = R_u/M. With M = 44 kg/kmol = 0.044 kg/mol and R_u = 8.314 J/(mol·K), R = 8.314/0.044 = 188.9 J/(kg·K), about 0.1889 kJ/(kg·K).

quiz.q: Why does attraction between molecules lower the measured pressure of a real gas?
quiz.a: A molecule about to strike the wall is pulled back by its neighbours, so it hits with less momentum. The wall therefore feels a smaller force per unit area than in an ideal gas.

quiz.q: Why is molar volume, not total volume, used in the van der Waals equation?
quiz.a: The constants a and b are quoted per mole. Writing the equation per mole keeps a and b fixed for a gas; for n moles the volume term is the total V and the equation is (p + an²/V²)(V − nb) = nRT.

quiz.q: One mole of CO₂ at 400 K occupies 0.030 m³. With a = 0.3640 Pa·m⁶/mol² and b = 4.267 × 10⁻⁵ m³/mol, find the ideal and the van der Waals pressure in kPa.
In a constant-volume gas thermometer the pressure at the triple point is 40.0 kPa. At the unknown state it reads 54.6 kPa. Find T.
At low pressure the van der Waals isotherm lies below the ideal isotherm; at very high pressure it lies above. Explain.
quiz.a: At low pressure molecules are far apart, so the b correction is negligible and the a/v² term dominates, reducing p below RT/v. At high pressure v is squeezed towards b, the free volume (v − b) becomes tiny and RT/(v − b) grows without limit, so repulsion dominates and p exceeds the ideal value.

beyond: Not for the exam. Cubic equations of state such as Peng–Robinson and Soave–Redlich–Kwong are the working tools in process simulators for refinery and fertiliser plant design, because they fit vapour-liquid equilibrium of mixtures. Above the critical point, supercritical carbon dioxide is used for extraction and for dry cleaning, where no ideal law applies. Real-gas data are compiled by NIST and by the International Association for the Properties of Water and Steam. Search for cubic equations of state, virial coefficients, and the law of corresponding states to go further.
